text: Acceptance criteria tell us what v1 does. This video draws the line around it — on paper, in writing — what's included, and just as importantly, what's deliberately deferred. This is the document you point back to three weeks from now when a great idea threatens to turn a six-week build into a ten-week build.

Every idea that came up in discovery but didn't make the acceptance criteria gets a real disposition — not a shrug. Labor-hours tracking: deferred, no clean source system yet. Payroll integration: rejected outright, that's not a BI problem. Nothing gets forgotten, because forgotten scope resurfaces later as a surprise.

One item actually moved the other direction. Year-over-year comparison looked like scope creep, but once we saw the star schema we're about to design, dim_date already supports it almost for free. Scoping isn't about saying no to everything — it's pricing each item honestly.

The deferred list gets framed as a visible v2 backlog, not a rejection letter. Riverside sees a roadmap, not a wall — a few solid ideas waiting for the next phase, written down so nobody worries they've been ignored.

We rehearse the scope-creep conversation before we need it. When the VP asks for labor-hours mid-build, the answer isn't no — it's "that's already on the v2 list, and pulling it into v1 costs about two weeks. Your call." That hands the tradeoff back to the person who should make it.

Get this boundary signed off the same way as the brief, and it becomes the thing we reopen at final handoff to show what shipped and what's next. With scope locked, we can finally pick the actual tools — SQL Server, SSIS, SSRS, and Power BI — next.
